title: Relational division for analytical questions
description: Learn how to answer analytical questions that ask which entities satisfy every requirement in a reference set, using relational division, anti-joins, and a small hypothetical retail dataset with counterexamples.
lead: Some analytical questions are not asking whether an entity has any matching record. They are asking whether the entity satisfies every member of a required set. That pattern is relational division. It appears in questions such as which customers bought every required item, which stores passed every audit check, which accounts have enabled every mandatory control, or which learners completed every course in a curriculum. The hard part is not writing a longer join. The hard part is preserving the meaning of “every” when there are duplicates, extra facts, missing facts, and filtered facts.

sections.heading: The shape of the question
paragraphs: Relational division is the relational counterpart to “for all.” Given one relation that records facts about entities and requirements, and another relation that lists the required values, division returns the entities that have a fact for every required value. In analytics, the entity is often a customer, account, store, user, supplier, or device. The requirement set might be mandatory products, required checks, required features, required forms, or required milestones.

A common mistake is to treat this as an “any match” problem. A join from customers to purchases to required products can tell you which required products were purchased. It does not, by itself, tell you which customers purchased all required products. Another mistake is to count rows without first deciding the grain. If duplicate purchase rows exist, row counts can make an incomplete customer look complete.

The prerequisite modeling idea is simple but important: the relationship being divided should be understood at a stable grain. For this article, the logical question is customer by SKU. A customer either has at least one qualifying fulfilled purchase of a required SKU, or does not. Duplicate qualifying rows do not create additional requirement coverage. Extra non-required SKUs do not hurt. Returned or canceled items are not qualifying facts because the business question here says “fulfilled purchase.”
bullets: Dividend relation: qualifying facts, such as fulfilled customer SKU purchases.
Divisor relation: the reference set, such as required SKUs.
Quotient result: entities that cover every value in the reference set.

sections.heading: A hypothetical retail fixture with counterexamples
paragraphs: The following illustrative SQL uses a small hypothetical retail dataset. It is written in ordinary PostgreSQL-style common table expressions using VALUES so the example is self-contained. No execution result is claimed; the expected result is worked through below.

The reference set contains three required SKUs: R100, R200, and R300. Ada has all three, plus a duplicate row for R300. Ben has R100 twice and R200 once, but is missing R300. Cy has all three and an extra SKU. Dia has R100 and R300, but R200 was returned. Eli has R100 and R300, but R200 was canceled. The intended answer is Ada and Cy only.
bullets: Ada qualifies because the duplicate does not matter and she covers all three required SKUs.
Ben does not qualify because duplicates of R100 cannot substitute for missing R300.
Cy qualifies because extra non-required SKU R999 does not disqualify him.
Dia and Eli do not qualify because returned and canceled rows are filtered out before evaluating coverage.

WITH
customers(customer_id, customer_name) AS (
  VALUES
    (1, 'Ada'),
    (2, 'Ben'),
    (3, 'Cy'),
    (4, 'Dia'),
    (5, 'Eli')
),
required_skus(sku) AS (
  VALUES
    ('R100'),
    ('R200'),
    ('R300')
),
purchase_items(customer_id, sku, status) AS (
  VALUES
    (1, 'R100', 'fulfilled'),
    (1, 'R200', 'fulfilled'),
    (1, 'R300', 'fulfilled'),
    (1, 'R300', 'fulfilled'),
    (2, 'R100', 'fulfilled'),
    (2, 'R100', 'fulfilled'),
    (2, 'R200', 'fulfilled'),
    (3, 'R100', 'fulfilled'),
    (3, 'R200', 'fulfilled'),
    (3, 'R300', 'fulfilled'),
    (3, 'R999', 'fulfilled'),
    (4, 'R100', 'fulfilled'),
    (4, 'R200', 'returned'),
    (4, 'R300', 'fulfilled'),
    (5, 'R100', 'fulfilled'),
    (5, 'R200', 'cancelled'),
    (5, 'R300', 'fulfilled')
)
SELECT *
FROM purchase_items;

sections.heading: Division with double NOT EXISTS
paragraphs: A direct way to express relational division in SQL is the double NOT EXISTS pattern. Read it inside out: for a given customer, there must not exist a required SKU for which there does not exist a qualifying fulfilled purchase. In plainer language, there is no missing required SKU.

This formulation is useful because it matches the semantics of “every.” It does not depend on row counts. It naturally ignores duplicate fulfilled rows because the inner EXISTS only asks whether at least one qualifying fact exists. It also ignores extra non-required facts because the outer loop is driven by the reference set, not by all purchased SKUs.

For the hypothetical fixture, Ada is returned because R100, R200, and R300 each have at least one fulfilled purchase for customer 1. Cy is returned for the same reason. Ben fails when the outer required SKU is R300. Dia fails when the required SKU is R200 because the only R200 row has status returned. Eli fails for R200 because the row is cancelled.

codeExamples.code:
WITH
customers(customer_id, customer_name) AS (
  VALUES
    (1, 'Ada'),
    (2, 'Ben'),
    (3, 'Cy'),
    (4, 'Dia'),
    (5, 'Eli')
),
required_skus(sku) AS (
  VALUES
    ('R100'),
    ('R200'),
    ('R300')
),
purchase_items(customer_id, sku, status) AS (
  VALUES
    (1, 'R100', 'fulfilled'),
    (1, 'R200', 'fulfilled'),
    (1, 'R300', 'fulfilled'),
    (1, 'R300', 'fulfilled'),
    (2, 'R100', 'fulfilled'),
    (2, 'R100', 'fulfilled'),
    (2, 'R200', 'fulfilled'),
    (3, 'R100', 'fulfilled'),
    (3, 'R200', 'fulfilled'),
    (3, 'R300', 'fulfilled'),
    (3, 'R999', 'fulfilled'),
    (4, 'R100', 'fulfilled'),
    (4, 'R200', 'returned'),
    (4, 'R300', 'fulfilled'),
    (5, 'R100', 'fulfilled'),
    (5, 'R200', 'cancelled'),
    (5, 'R300', 'fulfilled')
)
SELECT c.customer_id, c.customer_name
FROM customers AS c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM required_skus AS r
  WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM purchase_items AS p
    WHERE p.customer_id = c.customer_id
      AND p.sku = r.sku
      AND p.status = 'fulfilled'
  )
)
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

sections.heading: Division with EXCEPT
paragraphs: Another readable formulation is to compute the set of missing requirements per entity. For each customer, subtract the customer’s fulfilled SKUs from the required SKUs. If the result is empty, the customer satisfies every requirement.

In PostgreSQL, EXCEPT returns rows from the first query that are not returned by the second query, using set semantics unless EXCEPT ALL is specified. The illustrative query below therefore treats repeated fulfilled purchases as one covered SKU, which is what this analytical question needs. The same caution applies as before: filter the fact relation to qualifying rows before comparing it with the reference set.

The EXCEPT version can be easier to debug because the missing set can be inspected directly. If the final predicate says NOT EXISTS around the missing set, then a failing customer can be diagnosed by running the inner EXCEPT for that customer and seeing which requirement remains.

codeExamples.code:
WITH
customers(customer_id, customer_name) AS (
  VALUES
    (1, 'Ada'),
    (2, 'Ben'),
    (3, 'Cy'),
    (4, 'Dia'),
    (5, 'Eli')
),
required_skus(sku) AS (
  VALUES
    ('R100'),
    ('R200'),
    ('R300')
),
purchase_items(customer_id, sku, status) AS (
  VALUES
    (1, 'R100', 'fulfilled'),
    (1, 'R200', 'fulfilled'),
    (1, 'R300', 'fulfilled'),
    (1, 'R300', 'fulfilled'),
    (2, 'R100', 'fulfilled'),
    (2, 'R100', 'fulfilled'),
    (2, 'R200', 'fulfilled'),
    (3, 'R100', 'fulfilled'),
    (3, 'R200', 'fulfilled'),
    (3, 'R300', 'fulfilled'),
    (3, 'R999', 'fulfilled'),
    (4, 'R100', 'fulfilled'),
    (4, 'R200', 'returned'),
    (4, 'R300', 'fulfilled'),
    (5, 'R100', 'fulfilled'),
    (5, 'R200', 'cancelled'),
    (5, 'R300', 'fulfilled')
)
SELECT c.customer_id, c.customer_name
FROM customers AS c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT r.sku
  FROM required_skus AS r
  EXCEPT
  SELECT p.sku
  FROM purchase_items AS p
  WHERE p.customer_id = c.customer_id
    AND p.status = 'fulfilled'
)
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

sections.heading: The counting counterexample
paragraphs: Counting can be correct if the counted expression matches the logical grain, but a careless count is a common source of false positives. The following query is wrong for this problem because it counts rows, not distinct covered requirements. Ben has three fulfilled rows among required SKUs: R100, R100, and R200. A row count of three equals the number of required SKUs, so Ben would be incorrectly included despite missing R300.

This is the key modeling lesson: coverage is not the same as activity volume. A customer with many rows for one requirement may still be incomplete. A store with many passing checks in one category may still be missing another mandatory check. A user with many events for one onboarding step may still not have completed every step.

A count-based version can be repaired by counting distinct required values after applying the qualifying filter. Even then, be explicit about the reference set’s grain. If requirements are unique by SKU, count distinct SKU. If requirements are unique by jurisdiction and form type, count distinct pairs at that grain. If the reference table can contain duplicate requirement rows unintentionally, add a uniqueness constraint or derive a distinct reference set before division.

codeExamples.code:
-- Counterexample: this is wrong because duplicate rows can hide missing requirements.
WITH
required_skus(sku) AS (
  VALUES ('R100'), ('R200'), ('R300')
),
purchase_items(customer_id, sku, status) AS (
  VALUES
    (2, 'R100', 'fulfilled'),
    (2, 'R100', 'fulfilled'),
    (2, 'R200', 'fulfilled')
)
SELECT p.customer_id
FROM purchase_items AS p
WHERE p.status = 'fulfilled'
  AND p.sku IN (SELECT sku FROM required_skus)
GROUP BY p.customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM required_skus);

-- Safer count-based shape for a non-empty reference set.
-- The counted expression is the distinct requirement value, not the row count.
SELECT p.customer_id
FROM purchase_items AS p
JOIN required_skus AS r
  ON r.sku = p.sku
WHERE p.status = 'fulfilled'
GROUP BY p.customer_id
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT r.sku) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM required_skus);

sections.heading: Modeling decisions before querying
paragraphs: Before writing a division query, decide what belongs in the divisor and what counts as a matching fact. The divisor should be the authoritative reference set for the question. If the question is “which customers bought every required SKU in the starter kit,” then required_skus should contain the starter kit SKUs at the intended grain. If the question is “which accounts enabled every mandatory security control for their plan,” the divisor may depend on plan, region, or account type. That makes the reference set conditional, not global.

The qualifying fact relation should also be narrowed before division. In the example, only fulfilled purchase rows count. That filter is part of the semantics, not an optimization detail. If the filter is applied after division, returned or canceled rows can produce incorrect coverage. In dimensional models, this often means building or selecting a business-ready fact view whose grain and status rules are already clear.

Also decide how to handle an empty reference set. In classical logic, every entity satisfies every requirement in an empty set because there is no missing requirement. The double NOT EXISTS query follows that vacuous truth interpretation and would return all customers if required_skus were empty. That may be exactly right for some questions and surprising for others. If the business meaning requires at least one active requirement, enforce that separately with a data quality check or an explicit predicate.
bullets: Name the entity being returned.
Name the requirement set and its key.
Name the qualifying fact and its grain.
Filter facts before testing coverage.
Document the intended behavior when the requirement set is empty.

sections.heading: A diagnostic checklist for analytical division
paragraphs: When a query that should mean “every” produces suspicious results, inspect it using small counterexamples rather than a large dashboard aggregate. Add one entity with all requirements, one with a duplicate but a missing requirement, one with extra facts, and one with a non-qualifying status. If the query cannot classify those four cases correctly, it is not expressing relational division correctly.

Then inspect the keys. The reference set should not have accidental duplicates at the requirement grain. PostgreSQL documentation describes unique and primary key constraints as ways to enforce uniqueness in table definitions; the same modeling principle applies even when the example is implemented as a view or transformation. For production models, a required_skus table would usually have a key or uniqueness rule on sku, or on the full composite requirement grain.

Finally, separate semantic correctness from engine tuning. Indexes, join order, and materialization can matter for large data, but they should not change the answer. Start with the relational meaning: no required value is missing for the entity. Once the answer is correct on counterexamples, performance work can preserve that meaning at scale.
bullets: If duplicates change the answer, the query is probably counting rows instead of requirements.
If extras disqualify an entity, the query may be testing exact equality of sets when it should test containment.
If returned or canceled facts qualify, the status filter is in the wrong place or missing.
If an empty reference set returns surprising results, the business rule for empty requirements is undefined.

takeaways: Relational division answers “which entities satisfy every requirement in this reference set,” not “which entities have any matching row.”
Use double NOT EXISTS or an EXCEPT-based missing-set query to express “no required value is missing.”
Duplicates, extra facts, and non-qualifying statuses are the fastest way to find whether a query really models coverage.
Count-based solutions must count distinct requirement values at the correct grain, not fact rows.
Define the empty-reference-set behavior explicitly because the mathematically natural answer may not match business expectations.

title: Floating-point error in financial analytics
description: A practical guide to demonstrating representation error in repeated decimal arithmetic, using a hypothetical retail discount counterexample and explicit calculation rules.
lead: Floating-point error in financial analytics is easiest to understand when you stop treating it as a mysterious database or programming-language quirk and model it as a representation problem. Some decimal values that are ordinary in commerce, such as 0.10 dollars, do not have a finite binary fractional representation. If those approximations are stored or repeatedly aggregated, the residual can become visible in totals, reconciliations, and equality checks. This article uses a deliberately small hypothetical retail example and explicit arithmetic rules to show the mechanism without giving tax, accounting, or system-specific advice.

sections.heading: The reader problem: repeated decimal arithmetic looks exact until it is not
paragraphs: A data engineer may receive order events with line-item discounts, loyalty credits, refunds, or fees. The business concept is decimal: a 10-cent promotion is exactly 0.10 dollars, and 10,000 such promotions should total exactly 1,000.00 dollars. The analytics system, however, may represent the value with a binary floating-point type somewhere in the path: ingestion code, a transformation engine, a warehouse column, a feature store, or a notebook used for reconciliation.

The risk is not that every floating-point total will be visibly wrong. Modern binary floating-point formats are much finer than the toy model used below, and many reports round for display. The practical problem is subtler: values that are exact in the business domain can be approximate in the computational domain. Repetition, joins, regrouping, subtraction of nearly equal totals, and equality comparisons can expose the approximation.

PostgreSQL’s documentation makes the modeling distinction directly: numeric values can be stored with exact precision, while floating-point types are inexact. Its aggregate documentation also matters because totals are produced by aggregate functions whose return behavior depends on the input type. The durable lesson is not specific to PostgreSQL: before choosing a representation for financial analytics, make sure the representation matches the question you intend to answer.

sections.heading: Why 0.10 is not exactly representable as a finite binary fraction
paragraphs: A finite decimal fraction can be written as an integer divided by a power of 10. For example, 0.10 is 1/10, and 0.01 is 1/100. A finite binary fraction can be written as an integer divided by a power of 2. For example, 0.125 is 1/8, and 0.5 is 1/2.

Now ask whether 0.10 can be represented as a finite binary fraction. If it could, there would be integers k and n such that 1/10 = k / 2^n. Rearranging gives 10k = 2^n. The left side has a factor of 5 because 10 = 2 × 5. The right side is a power of 2 and has no factor of 5. That contradiction means no such finite binary representation exists.

The same argument applies to cents. One cent is 1/100. Since 100 = 2^2 × 5^2, a denominator of 100 contains factors of 5. A denominator that is only a power of 2 cannot exactly equal it after simplification. Some cent amounts are exactly representable in binary, such as 0.25 or 0.50 dollars, because their reduced fractions have denominators that are powers of 2. Many other ordinary amounts are not.

This proof does not depend on any particular database engine. It explains why a system using binary floating-point arithmetic must store a nearby value for many decimal amounts. The remaining engineering question is how to make that invisible approximation visible enough to reason about it.

sections.heading: A toy counterexample with explicit calculation rules
paragraphs: The following counterexample uses a hypothetical retail dataset and a deliberately coarse binary representation. It is not claiming that a production floating-point type stores values this coarsely. The point is to isolate the mechanism: repeated storage of a decimal value as a nearby binary fraction changes the aggregate.

Assume a retailer issues a 10-cent discount on every eligible order. The exact business amount per order is 0.10 dollars. To make representation error easy to calculate by hand, use this toy storage rule: every amount must be stored as an integer multiple of 1/1024 dollar, and each incoming amount is replaced by the nearest such multiple. If there is a tie, round upward. This is a binary fractional grid because 1024 is 2^10.

Now store 0.10 dollars. Since 0.10 × 1024 = 102.4, the nearest grid point is 102/1024, not 103/1024. The stored value is therefore 0.099609375 dollars. The per-row representation error is 0.099609375 - 0.10 = -0.000390625 dollars.

For 10,000 hypothetical discount rows, the exact business total is 10,000 × 0.10 = 1,000.00 dollars. If every row is first replaced by the toy binary approximation and then summed, the stored-row total is 10,000 × 0.099609375 = 996.09375 dollars. The residual is -3.90625 dollars.

That residual is intentionally large because the toy grid is coarse. A real double-precision binary float uses many more bits than this toy representation, so this example must not be read as a performance or accuracy benchmark for a particular type. Its value is diagnostic: it proves that repeated decimal arithmetic can accumulate representation error even when each individual input looked harmless.
bullets: Exact business value per row: 0.10 dollars.
Toy binary grid: multiples of 1/1024 dollar.
Stored toy value per row: 102/1024 = 0.099609375 dollars.
Per-row residual: -0.000390625 dollars.
Exact total for 10,000 rows: 1,000.00 dollars.
Toy stored-row total for 10,000 rows: 996.09375 dollars.
Aggregate residual: -3.90625 dollars.

codeExamples.code:
from fractions import Fraction

# Hypothetical retail discount: $0.10 per order.
# Toy representation rule: store each amount as the nearest multiple of 1/1024 dollar.
# This script uses exact rational arithmetic to demonstrate the representation step.

def quantize_to_1024(x: Fraction) -> Fraction:
    scaled = x * 1024
    # nearest integer, ties upward; all values in this example are positive
    units = (scaled.numerator * 2 + scaled.denominator) // (2 * scaled.denominator)
    return Fraction(units, 1024)

orders = 10_000
exact_each = Fraction(10, 100)
stored_each = quantize_to_1024(exact_each)
exact_total = exact_each * orders
stored_total = stored_each * orders
residual = stored_total - exact_total

print(f"exact_each={float(exact_each):.9f}")
print(f"stored_each={float(stored_each):.9f}")
print(f"exact_total={float(exact_total):.5f}")
print(f"stored_total={float(stored_total):.5f}")
print(f"residual={float(residual):.5f}")

# Expected output:
# exact_each=0.100000000
# stored_each=0.099609375
# exact_total=1000.00000
# stored_total=996.09375
# residual=-3.90625

sections.heading: What this example diagnoses in a real analytics pipeline
paragraphs: The toy example separates three concepts that are often blurred during pipeline debugging. First, there is the business value: the value domain says a discount is exactly 10 cents. Second, there is the stored representation: the computational domain may use a nearby binary value. Third, there is the aggregate: repeated arithmetic combines the stored values, not the business values you had in mind.

A useful diagnostic is to build an invariant using a representation that matches the business domain. For a hypothetical order-discount table, store or derive an integer-cent column and compare it with the floating-derived total. The invariant is simple: if every eligible order receives exactly 10 cents, then the cent total must equal eligible_order_count × 10. If a floating-derived dollars total is used, do not compare it with exact equality unless you intentionally chose a representation where exact equality is valid.

The diagnostic should be scoped narrowly. It is not a full accounting reconciliation, and it is not a recommendation about tax treatment, revenue recognition, or presentation rounding. It is a numeric-correctness check: can the pipeline preserve repeated decimal amounts well enough for the analytic question? If the question is financial and exact cents matter, an integer minor-unit representation or an exact decimal type is usually a better starting point than binary floating point.

In PostgreSQL terms, this distinction maps to documented type behavior: numeric is designed for exact numeric storage, while real and double precision are inexact floating-point types. Aggregate functions such as sum then operate over the chosen input type. The implementation details of a production schema, including decimal precision and scale, are a separate modeling decision. This article’s narrower purpose is to show why the distinction matters before that choice is made.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative PostgreSQL 18-style diagnostic sketch, not an executed result.
-- The goal is to compare an exact minor-unit invariant with a floating-derived total.

WITH hypothetical_orders(order_id, discount_cents) AS (
  VALUES
    (1, 10),
    (2, 10),
    (3, 10),
    (4, 10),
    (5, 10)
)
SELECT
  COUNT(*) AS order_count,
  SUM(discount_cents) AS exact_discount_cents,
  COUNT(*) * 10 AS expected_discount_cents,
  SUM(discount_cents)::numeric / 100 AS exact_discount_dollars,
  SUM((discount_cents::double precision) / 100.0) AS floating_derived_dollars
FROM hypothetical_orders;

sections.heading: A simple rule for practitioners
paragraphs: Use floating-point arithmetic when small representation differences are acceptable for the analytic purpose, such as many scientific, statistical, or approximate operational metrics. Be more cautious when the values are financial amounts, contractual quantities, ledger-like balances, or reconciliation inputs. In those domains, users often expect decimal identities to hold: 10,000 ten-cent discounts should reconcile to exactly 1,000.00 dollars before any explicitly defined rounding or adjustment.

The practical rule is: represent financial amounts in the smallest exact unit you need, or use an exact decimal type whose precision and scale are chosen deliberately. Then aggregate in that representation for reconciliation. Convert to a display format at the edge. If a floating-point value enters the pipeline because of a source system, file format, or modeling shortcut, add a diagnostic that compares it with an exact-domain invariant before the value becomes a trusted financial aggregate.

There is also a communication benefit. When an analyst sees a residual, the explanation should not be “computers are weird.” A better explanation is: the business value was a decimal fraction; the chosen computational representation was a binary approximation; repeated aggregation combined the approximations; here is the exact invariant that shows the difference. That explanation is testable and repairable.

Keep the scope disciplined. Choosing a decimal precision and scale, deciding where rounding should occur, and defining accounting policy are separate decisions. The representation-error demonstration only answers one foundational question: can repeated decimal arithmetic drift because the stored number is not the exact decimal number? Yes, and the counterexample above shows the mechanism.

takeaways: Many ordinary financial decimals, including 0.10 and 0.01, do not have finite binary fractional representations.
Repeated aggregation can expose representation error because the aggregate combines stored approximations, not the exact decimal values users have in mind.
A small hypothetical counterexample with explicit binary-grid rules is enough to demonstrate the mechanism without relying on a specific database result.
For financial analytics that must reconcile exactly, prefer integer minor units or exact decimal types, and use diagnostics that compare aggregates with exact-domain invariants.

title: Fixed-point decimal precision and scale
description: A practical guide to choosing DECIMAL precision and scale for stored facts and intermediate calculations, with worked capacity rules and a hypothetical retail-order example.
lead: Fixed-point decimal types are chosen twice: once for the values you store, and again for the calculations those values must survive. A column that fits every incoming price can still fail when prices are multiplied by quantities, summed across a batch, or squared for a statistical feature. The practical question is not “what DECIMAL type do we usually use?” It is “what maximum value, fractional detail, and intermediate expansion must this fact support?”

sections.heading: Precision, scale, and capacity are separate decisions
paragraphs: Most SQL systems expose fixed-point decimal numbers with a declaration like DECIMAL(p, s) or NUMERIC(p, s). PostgreSQL 18 documentation describes precision as the total count of significant digits and scale as the count of digits to the right of the decimal point. The remaining capacity, p minus s, is the number of digits available to the left of the decimal point.

That definition is simple, but the modeling consequence is easy to miss. DECIMAL(10, 2) is not “a money type.” It is a capacity promise: up to eight integer digits and two fractional digits, subject to the exact behavior of the database engine. A value such as 12345678.90 fits. A value such as 123456789.00 needs nine integer digits and does not fit. A value such as 12.345 has more fractional detail than the type stores.

For data engineering work, capacity should be selected from explicit assumptions. Those assumptions usually include the largest absolute stored value, the smallest unit of measurement that must be preserved, the largest group size used in aggregates, and the operations used in derived facts. This article focuses on representation and aggregation mechanics only. It does not provide tax, accounting, or financial policy advice.
bullets: Precision p: total digits available for the value, excluding sign and decimal separator.
Scale s: digits available after the decimal point.
Integer digit capacity: p minus s.
Stored value question: what is the largest absolute value and how many fractional digits must be preserved?
Intermediate question: how much can multiplication, summation, or other transformations expand the value before final storage?

sections.heading: Choose stored column capacity from range and fractional detail
paragraphs: Start with the physical fact being stored, not with a familiar default. A stored column needs enough integer digits for the largest value that should be valid, and enough fractional digits for the smallest unit that should survive ingestion. If a hypothetical retail order line stores a unit price up to 9,999.99, the price needs four integer digits and two fractional digits, so DECIMAL(6, 2) is the smallest matching declaration. If the unit price can reach 10,000.00, the integer requirement becomes five digits, so DECIMAL(7, 2) is the smallest matching declaration.

Quantities deserve the same treatment. A store that only sells whole units may model quantity as an integer. A store that sells fabric, produce, or fuel may need fractional units. If a hypothetical quantity can be as high as 999.999 units, it needs three integer digits and three fractional digits, so DECIMAL(6, 3) is the smallest matching declaration.

Avoid choosing scale from display formatting alone. A dashboard may show two decimals, but an upstream operational value may need three or six decimals to support later calculations. Conversely, preserving unnecessary fractional detail can make schemas harder to reason about and may increase storage or compute costs depending on the engine. The durable decision is not “more decimals are safer.” The durable decision is “store the detail the business fact actually carries, then explicitly choose where derived outputs are rounded.”
bullets: Rule 1: integer_digits = digits needed for the maximum absolute valid value before the decimal point.
Rule 2: scale = fractional digits needed for the smallest valid stored unit.
Rule 3: precision = integer_digits + scale.
Rule 4: keep the sign out of the precision calculation; negative values still need the same digit capacity as their absolute value.
Rule 5: document whether the declared maximum is a physical limit, a business rule, or only an observed historical maximum.

sections.heading: Intermediate calculations need their own capacity budget
paragraphs: A common failure mode is sizing every stored field correctly, then using the same size for derived fields. Multiplication and aggregation expand numeric capacity. If the intermediate result is held in a column, materialized model, staging table, or data frame with insufficient fixed-point capacity, the pipeline may overflow, truncate, or round earlier than intended.

For multiplication, add the integer capacities and add the scales. Suppose unit_price is DECIMAL(6, 2), so it has four integer digits and two fractional digits. Suppose quantity is DECIMAL(6, 3), so it has three integer digits and three fractional digits. The exact product can require seven integer digits and five fractional digits. The smallest fixed-point capacity for the unrounded product is DECIMAL(12, 5).

The arithmetic checks out at the boundary. The largest unit_price under DECIMAL(6, 2) is 9,999.99. The largest quantity under DECIMAL(6, 3) is 999.999. Their product is 9,999,980.00001. That value has seven integer digits and five fractional digits, exactly matching DECIMAL(12, 5).

For summation, keep the scale of the addends and add enough integer digits for the group size. If each line amount can have seven integer digits and five fractional digits, summing up to 250,000 lines can require 13 integer digits, because 250,000 introduces six orders of magnitude of expansion. The conservative rule is integer_digits_for_sum = integer_digits_of_addend + ceiling(log10(max_row_count)), with ceiling(log10(1)) treated as 0. The scale stays five if you are summing the unrounded line amounts.

That gives DECIMAL(18, 5) for the daily unrounded line sum: 13 integer digits plus five fractional digits. The boundary example is 9,999,980.00001 multiplied by 250,000, which equals 2,499,995,000,002.50000. A daily aggregate declared as DECIMAL(12, 2) would be too small by integer capacity, even though it looks like a large money field.
bullets: Multiplication rule: result integer digits = left integer digits + right integer digits; result scale = left scale + right scale.
Summation rule: result scale = addend scale; result integer digits = addend integer digits + ceiling(log10(maximum number of addends)).
Average rule: the average of nonnegative values does not exceed the maximum input value, but the sum used to compute it still needs summation capacity.
Subtraction rule: capacity usually matches the larger absolute input range, but signed results may need to be allowed even when both source columns are nonnegative.
Division rule: choose output scale deliberately; division can create repeating decimals, so the result scale is a modeling decision rather than a natural consequence of the inputs.

sections.heading: Worked example: hypothetical retail order facts
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail-order model with three values: unit_price, quantity, and daily gross merchandise value. The assumptions are intentionally explicit. Unit price is valid from 0.00 through 9,999.99. Quantity is valid from 0.000 through 999.999. A daily sales aggregate can include at most 250,000 order lines. The model wants to keep unrounded line arithmetic until the final aggregate is produced.

The stored unit_price requires four integer digits and two fractional digits, so DECIMAL(6, 2) is sufficient. The stored quantity requires three integer digits and three fractional digits, so DECIMAL(6, 3) is sufficient. Those two choices are fine for stored inputs, but neither is sufficient for the line amount. The unrounded line amount requires DECIMAL(12, 5), as shown by the boundary product 9,999.99 times 999.999 equals 9,999,980.00001.

Now size the daily aggregate. The largest possible unrounded line amount is 9,999,980.00001. The largest daily group has 250,000 lines. The maximum daily sum under those assumptions is 2,499,995,000,002.50000. That requires 13 integer digits and five fractional digits. Therefore the intermediate daily sum needs DECIMAL(18, 5) if it preserves the unrounded line scale.

A counterexample makes the risk concrete. Suppose a developer stores line_amount as DECIMAL(10, 2) because displayed currency has two decimals. The boundary product cannot be represented at full detail because it has seven integer digits and five fractional digits. Suppose another developer skips line storage but declares the daily aggregate as DECIMAL(12, 2). That aggregate allows only ten integer digits, so it cannot hold 2,499,995,000,002.50. Both schemas can pass casual tests with small orders and still fail under valid inputs.

The right final storage type may differ from the right intermediate type. If the published daily metric is intentionally defined at two decimal places, final storage might use two fractional digits after an explicit rounding rule. But the calculation leading to that final value still needs enough capacity for the unrounded product and the unrounded sum. Capacity design should make that distinction visible.
bullets: Input unit_price: DECIMAL(6, 2), based on 9,999.99 maximum.
Input quantity: DECIMAL(6, 3), based on 999.999 maximum.
Intermediate line_amount: DECIMAL(12, 5), based on multiplying price by quantity.
Intermediate daily sum for up to 250,000 lines: DECIMAL(18, 5).
Potential final reporting value: separately defined, with its own rounding and storage policy.

sections.heading: A diagnostic for existing decimal models
paragraphs: Existing warehouses often contain decimal choices that were copied from earlier tables. A quick diagnostic is to reverse engineer the implied assumptions and compare them with the business process. For every fixed-point fact, write down the largest representable positive value, the stored fractional unit, and the largest intermediate expression that uses it.

For a DECIMAL(10, 2) amount, the implied maximum is 99,999,999.99. That may be plenty for an order line and too small for a daily marketplace total. For a DECIMAL(8, 6) ratio, the implied maximum is 99.999999. That may fit a percentage stored as 0 to 1, but it may hide an unclear convention if some teams store 25 percent as 0.25 and others store it as 25.000000.

The diagnostic should also cover non-money facts. Kimball’s dimensional modeling guidance treats lags and durations as facts that can be stored and analyzed. A shipment duration, processing latency, energy usage measure, or model feature can have the same precision and scale problems as currency. Separately, be aware that “scale” also has a statistical meaning, such as measures of spread described by NIST. Decimal scale in DECIMAL(p, s) is about digits after the decimal point; statistical scale is about variability. Confusing the two can lead to unclear design conversations.
bullets: List every DECIMAL or NUMERIC column used as a fact, measure, or model feature.
For each column, compute integer digit capacity as precision minus scale.
State the largest valid source value, not just the largest value observed so far.
Trace multiplication, summation, averages, ratios, and squared terms that use the column.
Check whether staging tables and materialized aggregates have enough capacity for intermediate results, not only final display values.
Record the rounding point separately from the storage capacity decision.

sections.heading: Tradeoffs and practical defaults
paragraphs: The safest-looking type is not always the best model. Extremely wide decimals can obscure the real domain, allow impossible values, and make downstream contracts vague. Very narrow decimals create overflow and premature rounding risk. The useful middle ground is a documented capacity envelope: what the value means, how large it can be, how much fractional detail matters, and how calculations expand it.

When the true maximum is unknown, choose a defensible ceiling and label it as a business assumption. For example, “daily order lines are capped at 250,000 for this aggregate” is better than silently choosing DECIMAL(18, 2). If the ceiling changes, the schema can be reviewed with a known reason. This is especially important for backfills and migrations, where historical volume may exceed current operational expectations.

The core habit is to size facts from their domain and size calculations from their expressions. Stored unit_price, stored quantity, unrounded line_amount, daily sum, and published daily metric are different numeric artifacts. They may all describe the same business process, but they do not all need the same precision and scale.
bullets: Use narrow types when the domain is genuinely narrow and stable.
Use wider intermediate types when multiplication or aggregation expands capacity.
Do not rely on display formatting as a substitute for numeric modeling.
Treat maximum group size as part of the aggregate contract.
Document assumptions so future schema changes can be reviewed instead of guessed.

takeaways: DECIMAL(p, s) is a capacity contract: p is total digits, s is fractional digits, and p minus s is integer digit capacity.
Stored values and intermediate calculations should be sized separately; multiplication adds integer capacities and scales, while summation expands integer capacity by group size.
A schema can fit every input value and still fail on valid aggregates if intermediate line amounts or grouped sums are undersized.
Use explicit assumptions for maximum values, fractional units, and maximum row counts instead of copying a familiar decimal type.

title: Rounding at ingestion versus presentation
description: A practical guide to showing how rounding before or after aggregation changes reconciled totals, with explicit rules, a hypothetical retail example, and a diagnostic SQL pattern.
lead: Rounding is not just a display concern. If a pipeline rounds at ingestion and a report rounds at presentation, both can be internally consistent while producing different reconciled totals. The fix is not to declare one number “right” by habit. The fix is to define the grain, the stored measure, the aggregation rule, and the rounding stage explicitly.

sections.heading: The problem: rounding is a transformation, not formatting
paragraphs: A common reconciliation failure starts with two reasonable-sounding rules. One system stores each transaction line rounded to cents as soon as it arrives. Another system stores the unrounded decimal amount and rounds only the final report total. Neither rule is inherently irrational. The problem is that they answer different questions.

If the business question is “what is the sum of the displayed line amounts?”, then summing rounded line values is consistent. If the question is “what is the rounded value of the mathematically aggregated raw amounts?”, then rounding after aggregation is consistent. Those questions often appear under the same metric name, such as revenue, sales, charge amount, or net amount.

This article is limited to numeric representation and aggregation. It is not tax, invoicing, or accounting advice. Real organizations may have external rules that dictate the required rounding stage. The data engineering task is to make the rule visible, reproducible, and reconcilable instead of letting it emerge accidentally from pipeline order.

sections.heading: Two explicit rules that produce different totals
paragraphs: Use a deliberately small hypothetical retail dataset. Amounts are shown in dollars with three decimal places because upstream calculations can produce fractions of a cent after discounts, unit conversions, loyalty allocations, or currency-rate application. The example avoids half-cent ties so the result does not depend on a tie-breaking convention.

Define the rounding function for this example as ordinary rounding to two decimal places: 4.334 becomes 4.33, 2.336 becomes 2.34, and 13.002 becomes 13.00. The important point is not the name of the rounding mode. The important point is that the same rounding function is applied at different stages.

Rule A is ingestion rounding: round each line amount to two decimals when loading the line fact, then aggregate the stored rounded line amount. Rule B is presentation rounding: store the unrounded decimal line amount, aggregate those unrounded values, then round the final result for display.

Consider order O1001 with three line amounts: 4.334, 4.334, and 4.334. Under Rule A, each line becomes 4.33 and the order total is 12.99. Under Rule B, the raw sum is 13.002 and the displayed order total is 13.00. The same source lines reconcile to different order totals, with a difference of 0.01.

Now consider order O1002 with three line amounts: 2.336, 2.336, and 2.336. Under Rule A, each line becomes 2.34 and the order total is 7.02. Under Rule B, the raw sum is 7.008 and the displayed order total is 7.01. The difference is again 0.01, but in the opposite direction.

At the daily grain, these two orders can appear to reconcile by coincidence. The rounded-at-ingestion total is 12.99 plus 7.02, or 20.01. The rounded-at-presentation total is round(13.002 plus 7.008, 2), which is round(20.010, 2), or 20.01. A daily reconciliation can pass while the order-level reconciliation fails. That is why rounding diagnostics need to run at the grain where users compare numbers, not only at the highest summary level.
bullets: Rule A: rounded_line_amount = round(raw_line_amount, 2); order_total = sum(rounded_line_amount).
Rule B: order_total = round(sum(raw_line_amount), 2).
For O1001, Rule A returns 12.99 and Rule B returns 13.00.
For O1002, Rule A returns 7.02 and Rule B returns 7.01.
For the two-order daily total, both rules return 20.01, masking the order-level differences.

sections.heading: A diagnostic query for finding rounding-stage differences
paragraphs: The following PostgreSQL 18 example is illustrative. It uses a hypothetical inline dataset and exact numeric values so the arithmetic is about rounding stage, not binary floating-point representation. PostgreSQL documentation describes numeric as an exact numeric type suitable when exactness is needed, and its aggregate documentation covers SUM as the standard aggregation function used here.

The diagnostic groups by the reconciliation grain, computes both candidate totals, and reports the delta. In a real model, the group by columns should match the grain at which totals are compared: order, invoice, statement, customer-month, store-day, or another explicitly defined grain.

The expected results for the hypothetical rows are: O1001 has sum_of_rounded_lines 12.99, rounded_sum_of_raw_lines 13.00, and delta -0.01. O1002 has 7.02, 7.01, and delta 0.01. If the same query is grouped only by sales_date, the delta for the two rows together is 0.00, demonstrating why a passing high-level check does not prove lower-grain reconciliation.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative PostgreSQL 18 example; not execution evidence.
-- Hypothetical retail line amounts.
with line_amounts as (
    select *
    from (values
        ('2026-10-26'::date, 'O1001', 'L1', 4.334::numeric),
        ('2026-10-26'::date, 'O1001', 'L2', 4.334::numeric),
        ('2026-10-26'::date, 'O1001', 'L3', 4.334::numeric),
        ('2026-10-26'::date, 'O1002', 'L1', 2.336::numeric),
        ('2026-10-26'::date, 'O1002', 'L2', 2.336::numeric),
        ('2026-10-26'::date, 'O1002', 'L3', 2.336::numeric)
    ) as t(sales_date, order_id, line_id, raw_line_amount)
)
select
    sales_date,
    order_id,
    sum(round(raw_line_amount, 2)) as sum_of_rounded_lines,
    round(sum(raw_line_amount), 2) as rounded_sum_of_raw_lines,
    sum(round(raw_line_amount, 2)) - round(sum(raw_line_amount), 2) as rounding_stage_delta
from line_amounts
group by sales_date, order_id
order by sales_date, order_id;

sections.heading: Why aggregate tables magnify the issue
paragraphs: Rounding-stage choices become harder to see when teams introduce summary tables. Dimensional models often use aggregate fact tables or cubes to store summarized data for performance or usability. That design can be appropriate, but it makes the derivation rule part of the contract. A store-day aggregate built from rounded order totals is not the same measure as a store-day aggregate built from raw line amounts and then rounded.

The dangerous version is not “we rounded.” The dangerous version is “different layers rounded differently while using the same metric name.” A detail table might expose raw_line_amount. A mart table might expose line_amount_cents rounded at ingestion. A dashboard semantic layer might define revenue as round(sum(raw_line_amount), 2). A finance extract might define revenue as sum(line_amount_cents). Those can all look plausible in isolation.

A useful aggregate table definition states its source grain and its calculation rule. For example: customer_day_revenue.display_amount is calculated as round(sum(order_line.raw_net_amount), 2) grouped by customer_id and sales_date. Or: customer_day_revenue.booked_amount is calculated as sum(order_line.rounded_net_amount) grouped by customer_id and sales_date. Those two measures should not silently share the same name unless the organization has accepted the difference and documented why it is immaterial or required.

The same principle applies to reconciliation tests. A check that compares an aggregate table to detail should use the same rounding stage as the aggregate table. If the aggregate stores sum of rounded lines, compare it to sum(round(raw_line_amount, 2)). If the aggregate stores rounded sum of raw lines, compare it to round(sum(raw_line_amount), 2). Mixing the check can create false incidents or, worse, normalize a hidden metric definition mismatch.

sections.heading: Implementation pattern: store both intent and calculation stage
paragraphs: A robust model separates the source measurement from the reported measurement. The source measurement preserves the best available numeric value at the event or line grain. The reported measurement applies the agreed rounding rule at the agreed stage. This does not require every downstream user to reason from first principles every time; it requires the model to name the difference.

For example, a line fact can include raw_net_amount as the unrounded decimal measure received or calculated by the ingestion process. It can also include rounded_net_amount if the business process requires line-level display or line-level reconciliation. A derived order model can then expose order_net_amount_from_rounded_lines and order_net_amount_rounded_after_sum during validation. Once the policy is settled, the public metric can choose one, but the validation columns make the choice inspectable.

Avoid using column names that hide the stage. amount, total, net, and revenue are too vague when multiple rounding stages exist. Better names include raw_line_amount, rounded_line_amount, sum_of_rounded_line_amount, and rounded_sum_raw_line_amount. Verbose names are not elegant, but they reduce ambiguity in reconciliation conversations.

This pattern also helps with incident triage. When a stakeholder reports that a dashboard is off by a few cents from an export, the first diagnostic question becomes mechanical: are both outputs summing the same stored measure and rounding at the same grain? If not, the difference may be a definition mismatch rather than a data loss problem.
bullets: Preserve an unrounded decimal measure where the source and storage design allow it.
Create rounded measures only with a named rounding stage and grain.
Do not give ingestion-rounded and presentation-rounded measures the same metric name without a documented policy.
Run reconciliation at the lowest grain where users expect equality, not only at the dashboard total.
Treat small cent-level differences as explainable, not automatically acceptable; the rule still needs to be explicit.

sections.heading: Counterexample: “rounding only affects pennies” is not a rule
paragraphs: It is tempting to dismiss these differences because each group often differs by only a cent. That shortcut fails for two reasons. First, the direction is data-dependent. Values just below a rounding threshold tend to reduce totals when rounded per line; values just above a threshold tend to increase them. The net effect can cancel, accumulate, or vary by product, channel, or time period.

Second, reconciliation is often contractual at a specific grain. If customers, orders, invoices, or statements are displayed at a rounded amount, then a report that aggregates a different rounded representation may not tie back to those displayed records. The issue is not only materiality at the grand total. It is whether the model can explain the path from detail to summary.

A better shortcut is to keep a small diagnostic table or query that shows both totals and the delta by grain. If the delta is always zero, the chosen dataset is not proving much; try groups with repeated fractional-cent values around rounding thresholds. If the delta is nonzero, the team can decide which rule represents the metric and encode that rule consistently.

sections.heading: A concise decision checklist
paragraphs: Use this checklist when defining or reviewing a metric that can contain fractions smaller than the display unit. The goal is not to make every metric use the same rule. The goal is to make each metric use one rule intentionally.

First, identify the atomic grain of the source values. Is the amount born at event, line, order, allocation, usage interval, or customer-day grain? Second, identify the reconciliation grain. Where do users expect equality: line, order, statement, day, month, or report total? Third, choose whether the official metric sums rounded values or rounds after summing raw values. Fourth, ensure aggregate tables, semantic-layer metrics, extracts, and dashboards implement the same rule. Fifth, write a regression check that computes the alternative rule and reports the delta, so future changes do not move the rounding stage accidentally.

The durable lesson is simple: rounding stage is part of metric definition. If it is omitted, the pipeline still chooses a stage through implementation order. Practitioners should make that choice explicit before building aggregates that people will reconcile.

takeaways: Rounding at ingestion and rounding at presentation can both be internally consistent while producing different reconciled totals.
A reconciliation check must run at the grain where users expect numbers to tie; higher-level totals can hide lower-grain rounding differences.
Aggregate fact tables and semantic metrics should document whether they sum rounded values or round after summing raw values.
Use explicit measure names and diagnostic queries to make rounding-stage deltas visible instead of treating cent-level differences as mysterious pipeline noise.

title: Integer overflow in aggregate calculations
description: A practical guide to estimating intermediate numeric bounds in aggregate calculations, using a hypothetical retail example and explicit rules for products, sums, rollups, and ratios.
lead: Integer overflow in aggregate calculations is easy to miss because the raw column values can look safe. A price in cents, a quantity, a count, or a score may fit comfortably in an integer column, while the expression built from those columns does not. The practical fix is not only to check input ranges. Estimate the largest intermediate value produced by each multiplication, sum, rollup, and ratio component before choosing the data type.

sections.heading: Why input ranges are not enough
paragraphs: A common numeric review asks whether each stored column can hold the largest expected input. That is necessary, but it is not sufficient for aggregates. Aggregates create new values: a line amount, a daily total, a monthly rollup, a weighted numerator, or a denominator. Those intermediate values can be much larger than any single input field.

For example, PostgreSQL documents integer, bigint, decimal, numeric, real, and double precision numeric types, and its aggregate documentation describes widened return types for some sums. Those details matter, but they do not remove the modeling task. If an expression overflows before it reaches the aggregate, or if a rollup table stores a total in a narrower type than the aggregate produced, the result can still be wrong or fail.

The data engineering question is: what is the largest plausible value at each step of the calculation? The answer depends on grain. A per-order-line amount has a different bound from a store-day total, and a store-month aggregate fact table has a different bound again. Kimball’s aggregate fact table guidance is useful background here: aggregate tables summarize facts at a higher grain, so the numeric capacity should be chosen for that higher grain rather than copied from the base transaction grain.

sections.heading: A small counterexample
paragraphs: Suppose a hypothetical retail order-line table stores unit_price_cents and quantity as integer columns. The product unit_price_cents times quantity is used as line_revenue_cents. Each input value may fit within a 32-bit signed integer. That does not prove the product fits.

Use a deliberately small counterexample. A unit price of 999,999 cents is $9,999.99. A quantity of 3,000 is large, but not impossible for wholesale or bulk orders. Both inputs are far below 2,147,483,647, the maximum value of a common signed 32-bit integer. Their product is 2,999,997,000 cents, which is greater than 2,147,483,647. The input columns fit; the intermediate product does not.

There is a second failure mode. Even when the line product fits, the group sum may not. If the maximum line amount is 5,000,000 cents and a store-day group can contain 800,000 lines, the maximum store-day sum is 4,000,000,000,000 cents. That is well beyond 32-bit integer range. The column-level review would miss this unless it considered group size.

This article is not tax or accounting advice, and it does not address rounding allocation residuals or division-by-zero policy. The narrower point is numeric capacity: model the values your calculations create, not only the values you ingest.
bullets: Input bound: unit_price_cents <= 999,999 and quantity <= 3,000.
Intermediate product bound: 999,999 x 3,000 = 2,999,997,000 cents.
A 32-bit signed integer maximum is 2,147,483,647, so the product can exceed the type even though both inputs fit.
Aggregate bound: 800,000 lines x 5,000,000 cents = 4,000,000,000,000 cents.

sections.heading: Worked hypothetical retail example
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retailer that wants a store_month_sales aggregate table. The base fact grain is one order line. The aggregate grain is store_id plus calendar_month. The measure is gross_sales_cents, calculated from unit_price_cents times quantity. The following assumptions are intentionally conservative and self-contained; they are not customer results or benchmark data.

Assume the maximum unit price is 25,000 cents, the maximum quantity per line is 200, the maximum number of order lines per store per day is 800,000, a month has at most 31 days, and the aggregate covers one store-month. First estimate the line expression. The maximum line amount is 25,000 x 200 = 5,000,000 cents. Then estimate the store-day total. The maximum store-day total is 800,000 x 5,000,000 = 4,000,000,000,000 cents. Then estimate the store-month total. The maximum store-month total is 31 x 4,000,000,000,000 = 124,000,000,000,000 cents.

That final number is 124 trillion cents, or $1.24 trillion. The value may be an intentionally extreme operational bound, but that is the point of the exercise. If this number is impossible under real business constraints, document the stronger constraint and use it. If it is merely rare, the storage type still needs to handle it or the pipeline needs an explicit rejection rule.

Now compare this bound with common integer capacities. It is far too large for 32-bit integer. It fits within a 64-bit signed integer, whose positive maximum is about 9.22 quintillion. If future rollups combine many stores, currencies, or years, repeat the calculation at that new grain. Do not assume a type that fits the store-month table also fits an all-company multi-year table.

The main modeling decision is where to widen. A safe pattern is to cast before the multiplication and keep the aggregate storage type at least as wide as the largest estimated output. In PostgreSQL, numeric can be used for exact arbitrary-precision-style decimal calculations within documented limits, and the PostgreSQL aggregate documentation should be consulted for the exact return type of sum for the input expression being aggregated.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative PostgreSQL 18-oriented bound calculation.
-- This estimates capacity needs; it is not a claim of executed test results.
WITH assumptions AS (
  SELECT
    25000::numeric AS max_unit_price_cents,
    200::numeric AS max_quantity,
    800000::numeric AS max_lines_per_store_day,
    31::numeric AS max_days_per_month
), bounds AS (
  SELECT
    max_unit_price_cents * max_quantity AS max_line_sales_cents,
    max_lines_per_store_day * max_unit_price_cents * max_quantity AS max_store_day_sales_cents,
    max_days_per_month * max_lines_per_store_day * max_unit_price_cents * max_quantity AS max_store_month_sales_cents
  FROM assumptions
)
SELECT
  max_line_sales_cents,
  max_store_day_sales_cents,
  max_store_month_sales_cents
FROM bounds;

sections.heading: Rules for estimating intermediate bounds
paragraphs: The following rules are intentionally mechanical. They are meant to be applied during data modeling, code review, and metric definition review.

Rule 1: Bound expressions, not just columns. If the metric is sum(unit_price_cents * quantity), estimate the product first, then estimate the sum. Aggregate widening does not help if an earlier expression has already exceeded its safe range in the engine or intermediate representation being used.

Rule 2: Include group cardinality. A sum’s upper bound is not the maximum input value. It is the maximum number of rows in the group times the maximum contribution per row. If groups are uneven, use the largest plausible group, not the average group. Average line count per store-day is not a safe substitute for maximum line count per store-day.

Rule 3: Recompute bounds when the grain changes. Daily, monthly, store-level, regional, and all-company aggregates are different numeric objects. Aggregate fact tables and cubes are often built for performance and usability, but their measures still need type choices based on their summarized grain.

Rule 4: Treat weighted calculations as two aggregates. A weighted average such as sum(score_micro * event_count) / sum(event_count) has a numerator and a denominator. The final average may be between 0 and 1,000,000 micro-units, but the numerator can be enormous. Choosing a type based on the final displayed ratio is a category error.

Rule 5: Preserve sign assumptions explicitly. If returns, credits, or adjustments can be negative, calculate both lower and upper bounds. A signed type may need capacity for large negative totals as well as large positive totals. If business rules say a value cannot be negative, enforce that rule near ingestion or transformation, not only in a wiki page.

Rule 6: Add a margin for uncertainty, but do not hide the math. A capacity decision should say something like: maximum line amount is 5,000,000 cents; maximum group size is 800,000 lines; maximum month length is 31 days; bound is 124,000,000,000,000 cents; chosen type supports at least that value. The assumptions are reviewable, and future changes have somewhere concrete to attach.

sections.heading: Diagnostic query patterns
paragraphs: A diagnostic query can make the assumptions visible. It should not only scan current data for today’s maximum value. Current data may not contain tomorrow’s largest group. Use diagnostics for two different jobs: profile observed data, and compare documented bounds with type limits.

Observed profiling helps find surprises. For example, a store-day with far more order lines than expected may indicate a legitimate operating condition, duplicated records, or a bad join. Bound checks are different: they encode the maximum values the model claims to support.

The next example is illustrative. It profiles a hypothetical order_lines table and deliberately casts before multiplying. The cast is not about making the sample query pretty; it documents that the expression’s capacity is wider than the raw integer columns. In a production implementation, adapt the types, date functions, and limit values to the SQL engine and warehouse standards being used.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative profiling query for a hypothetical retail order_lines table.
-- Adapt date truncation and numeric types to the target SQL engine.
SELECT
  store_id,
  CAST(order_ts AS date) AS order_date,
  COUNT(*) AS line_count,
  MAX(unit_price_cents) AS observed_max_unit_price_cents,
  MAX(quantity) AS observed_max_quantity,
  MAX(CAST(unit_price_cents AS numeric) * CAST(quantity AS numeric)) AS observed_max_line_sales_cents,
  SUM(CAST(unit_price_cents AS numeric) * CAST(quantity AS numeric)) AS observed_store_day_sales_cents
FROM order_lines
GROUP BY store_id, CAST(order_ts AS date)
ORDER BY observed_store_day_sales_cents DESC
FETCH FIRST 20 ROWS ONLY;

-- Illustrative model check for documented assumptions.
-- The expected result is that store_month_bound_exceeds_int32 is true
-- and store_month_bound_exceeds_int64 is false for these assumptions.
WITH limits AS (
  SELECT
    2147483647::numeric AS int32_max,
    9223372036854775807::numeric AS int64_max
), assumptions AS (
  SELECT
    25000::numeric AS max_unit_price_cents,
    200::numeric AS max_quantity,
    800000::numeric AS max_lines_per_store_day,
    31::numeric AS max_days_per_month
), bound AS (
  SELECT
    max_unit_price_cents * max_quantity * max_lines_per_store_day * max_days_per_month AS max_store_month_sales_cents
  FROM assumptions
)
SELECT
  max_store_month_sales_cents,
  max_store_month_sales_cents > int32_max AS store_month_bound_exceeds_int32,
  max_store_month_sales_cents > int64_max AS store_month_bound_exceeds_int64
FROM bound CROSS JOIN limits;

sections.heading: Choosing the storage type
paragraphs: After estimating bounds, choose types for three places: the expression, the aggregate result, and the stored aggregate table. These can be different. A base table may store unit_price_cents as integer, the transformation may cast operands to numeric or bigint before multiplication, and the aggregate table may store gross_sales_cents as bigint or numeric depending on the calculated bound and the database’s documented behavior.

For exact money-like integer cents, integer arithmetic is often preferable to binary floating-point for the stored measure. A related background issue is floating-point error in financial analytics: floats can introduce representation surprises even when overflow is not the problem. This article’s focus is narrower. The immediate concern is whether the exact integer or decimal representation has enough capacity for every intermediate value.

Do not choose the smallest type that fits the sample data. Choose a type that fits the documented bound. If the documented bound is implausibly high, improve the model by adding a real constraint: maximum supported quantity, maximum supported unit price, maximum rows per batch, maximum stores per rollup, or maximum years retained in one aggregate. A constraint that is enforced by validation can reduce the numeric bound. A hope that the value will not get large cannot.

Also consider failure behavior. Some systems raise errors on overflow; others may wrap, saturate, or produce engine-specific behavior depending on the operation and type. The portable modeling practice is to avoid reaching the boundary at all, cast before risky expressions, and include checks that make unexpectedly large values visible before they corrupt downstream tables.
bullets: Use the base column type for valid inputs.
Use a wider expression type for products and weighted numerators.
Use an aggregate storage type sized for the output grain, not the input grain.
Document assumptions next to the model or metric definition so future grain changes trigger a capacity review.

takeaways: Check the largest value created by each expression, not only the largest value accepted by each input column.
For sums, estimate maximum contribution per row times maximum rows per group; for rollups, repeat the calculation at the new aggregate grain.
Cast before risky multiplications or weighted numerators, and store aggregate facts in a type sized for the documented bound.
